title: Who answers the distressed
hookLine: who answers the one in distress when he calls, and removes the evil (27:62)

lines: A RUN OF QUESTIONS IN AN-NAML.
cards: The car skids on ice. The doctor walks in with a face that's too careful. In that second, before any thinking, some people who rarely pray hear themselves say please, God.
Not a formal prayer. Just a call, with nothing else left to try. Near the end of An-Naml, a run of questions about the signs of God reaches exactly that moment.

teach.h: IS THERE A GOD BESIDE GOD?
teach.b: The passage goes like a drumbeat. Who created the heavens and the earth, sent down rain and grew gardens with it? Is there a god beside God?
Who made the earth a fixed place, ran rivers through it, set the mountains, and put a barrier between the two seas? Is there a god beside God?
Then verse sixty-two: who answers the one in distress when he calls on Him, and removes the evil, and makes you successors on the earth? Is there a god beside God?
The word for the distressed is al-mudtarr. The classical dictionaries give it the sense of being forced, driven into a corner: not just sad, but with no other options left.
The verse doesn't say the righteous, or the one who prays perfectly. It says the cornered one, when he calls.
Some commentators link it to another passage, where people in a storm at sea call on God sincerely and then, safe on land, forget.

The call itself is heard. That's why the verse sits among the signs, with rain and rivers and mountains: being answered in a corner is offered as something people know from their own lives, as plain as weather.
A hadith in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi names three prayers answered without doubt: of the one who is wronged, of the traveler, and of a parent.
Muslim teachers add that being answered doesn't always mean getting exactly what was asked. In their reading, the verse promises that the call is heard.

how: Many Muslims recite 27:62 in times of trouble and call on God in their own words in du'a, believing that the prayer of the one in distress is heard.

o: someone who prays perfectly, every single time
the one driven into a corner, with no way out
a traveler far from home on a long road

games.q: who answers the distressed — tap the pairs.
p: the one forced into a corner
is there a god beside God?
the wronged, the traveler, a parent

s: the verse says God answers only the righteous
it says the one in distress, when he calls.
al-mudtarr means someone forced, with no other options
the root is about being compelled, driven into a corner.
the verse sits among the signs of creation
it comes in a run of questions about rain, rivers and mountains.

games.q: you're out of options, and you've never been much for prayer. what does the verse say happens if you call?
o: nothing; you have to earn it first.
He answers the one in distress when they call.
games.why: 27:62 names God as the one who answers the distressed when he calls, and removes the evil.

practice: Find the worry that sits under everything this week, and name it plainly in your own words, without trying to solve it. If you pray, call on God with it now, in whatever language comes, the way the verse describes.
If you don't, say it out loud to the quiet, and set it down for this minute.

wordCard.voice: Al-mudtarr. The cornered, distressed one, named in An-Naml's question of who answers them when they call and lifts the harm. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the one in distress, from a root meaning forced or compelled.

carryVoice: Your line: he answers the distressed. Even a call from a corner is heard. Go gently.

sources.ref: Sunan Abi Dawud 1536; Jami' at-Tirmidhi 1905 (three answered prayers)
